Peace, Peace; When There Is No Peace
PEES PEES wen thair iz NOH PEES
n. phr. (Jeremiah's charge against the false prophets, Jeremiah 6:14)
Hebrew shālōm shālōm w''ēn shālōm — the doubling is emphatic, the manner of a confident proclamation; shālōm is wholeness and welfare, not merely the absence of war.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The charge stands twice in Jeremiah, in the same words: They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace. The figure is medical. A wound is treated on the surface, bound up and pronounced well while the infection goes on underneath, and the physician who does it is not merely mistaken but guilty, because the patient would have sought real help had he been told the truth. Jeremiah names the culprits exactly: from the prophet even unto the priest, every one dealeth falsely. These were not pagans but Judah's own clergy, saying what the people wanted and what the court rewarded, while Babylon marched. Ezekiel gives the same indictment a different image — a wall built badly and daubed with untempered morter, which looks sound until the overflowing shower brings it down. The sin is not optimism but false assurance: telling people they are at peace with God when they are not, and so removing the alarm that might have driven them to repent. The test Jeremiah applies is in the preceding verse: the false prophets were covetous and dealt falsely, and in the chapter before, the people loved to have it so.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Peace, a state of quiet or tranquillity; freedom from war; reconciliation with God. Slightly, superficially; with little care. Jeremiah 6:14, the wound healed on the surface.

expand to see more

Peace, in a Scriptural sense, reconciliation with God; spiritual peace of conscience.

Peace, freedom from war, from agitation, or from disturbance.

Slightly, superficially; with little care; in a trifling manner.

Hebrew shālōm, wholeness, welfare, soundness, peace.

Untempered morter, Ezekiel 13:10, the daubing that cannot bear the shower.

Key Scripture

Jer 6:13 — "For from the least of them even unto the greatest of them every one is given to covetousness; and from the prophet even unto the priest every one dealeth falsely."

Jer 6:14 — "They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace."

Jer 8:11 — "For they have healed the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace."

Eze 13:10 — "Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there was no peace; and one built up a wall, and, lo, others daubed it with untempered morter:"

Modern Corruption

The rebuke is turned against any preaching of comfort at all, breeding a ministry of perpetual severity; or it is applied only to other men's pulpits while the same false assurance is given under gentler words.

expand to see more

The verse is a favourite with those who have concluded that a faithful ministry must always wound. But Jeremiah is not condemning the announcement of peace — the same book promises a new covenant, and the same prophet is told to build and to plant as well as to root out. He is condemning the announcement of peace where there is none. A preacher who cannot comfort the afflicted has not escaped the error; he has only reversed it, and the sufferer he leaves without the gospel is as badly served as the impenitent who is told all is well.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is how the thing actually happens now. Almost no one says the words; the false peace is given by omission — by a gospel presentation that never mentions sin, by a counselling that treats guilt as a feeling to be managed rather than a verdict to be answered, by the quiet retirement of judgment, hell and repentance from the ordinary diet of preaching. The daughter of Jeremiah's people was not told she was fine; she was told everything except what was wrong with her, which came to the same thing when Babylon arrived.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shālōm doubled for emphasis — a confident proclamation of welfare over a wound healed only on the surface.

expand to see more

Hebrew shālōm, wholeness, soundness, welfare; more than the absence of war.

The doubling is the manner of confident public proclamation.

Hebrew rāphā', to heal; qālal, lightly or slightly — a superficial cure.

The same charge stands twice: Jeremiah 6:14 and Jeremiah 8:11.

Ezekiel's parallel figure is the wall daubed with untempered morter, Ezekiel 13:10.

Usage

"saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace"
